findings.text: Alarm management over the virtio RTC request queue for a selected clock. Reading reports the device alarm moment and whether it is enabled. Setting programs moment plus enabled state. Enabling toggles only the enabled state. Each operation reports device exchange status to the caller.

Cross timestamp and capability discovery for a selected clock and hardware counter. One operation returns a paired device reading and counter value. Another reports whether that pairing is supported. Discovery of clock count and per-clock attributes is also available through the request queue.

RTC class lifecycle for the virtio RTC device. Initialization creates a class instance bound to a parent device and clock identity with alarm availability decided by the caller. Registration publishes it to the RTC core. Stopping marks it stopped. Alarm delivery forwards a device event for the matching clock.

PTP clock provisioning for a virtio RTC clock. Registration creates a per-clock instance named by the caller and publishes it to the PTP core, adjusting cross timestamp support based on probing. A weak hardware hook supplies platform counter parameters and by default reports lack of support.
Per-queue state pairs the underlying virtio queue with its own spinlock for serialization of queue access and callback control.

Core device state links the virtio device and optional RTC class instance, holds per-queue states indexed by queue role, tracks clocks pending unregister, alarm input buffers with their count, and total clock count.

Request message state holds a back pointer to the device, opaque request and response buffers, a completion signaled on device reply, a shared ownership count, configured sizes, and the observed reply length.

Temporary on-stack request handle groups a message pointer with typed request and response views, their sizes, and a message identifier. Creation leaves views empty and records sizes and identifier for later allocation and typed access.

Queue callbacks serialize queue inspection and callback enable control under the per-queue spinlock with interrupts saved, then drop the lock before dispatching payload handling. Alarm reposting and kick preparation reuse the same lock.

RTC class state changes use the RTC core lock. Stopping publishes the stopped indication while holding that lock. Alarm read and update entry points operate on a locked class instance obtained from the device.

Request exchange owns a message with two initial references. Completion is signaled when the device returns the buffer and its length is recorded. Both the waiter and the completion path release once, freeing the last holder.

Queue callback draining disables callbacks once, repeatedly collects pending buffers, and reenables when empty, exiting only when reenabling confirms no missed event. Collected buffers are handled outside the lock before draining resumes.

Alarm notification handling validates length and type before extracting clock identity and forwarding. The input buffer is always returned to the device queue afterwards, with a host notification issued only when the queue requests it.

Wire values use little endian with width-specific conversion. Narrow byte values pass unchanged while wider values convert between host and device order, selected by the type of the value or the destination member.

Alarm moments cross layers in different units. The device uses nanoseconds while the RTC core uses broken-down time. Reading divides and converts, setting converts back and rejects negative times and overflowing multiplications.
Alarm enablement is carried as a single flag bit in device messages. Reading maps the bit to a boolean, setting and toggling construct the bit from the requested boolean.
Alarm events are filtered by clock identity. A mismatch is logged at a limited rate and dropped. When class support is compiled out, delivery is a no-op.

RTC class creation is restricted to smeared UTC clocks with at most one instance. Alarm availability requires class configuration, device feature, and per-clock capability together, and enables device wakeup. Update interrupts are never advertised and the supported range spans the full nanosecond counter expressed in seconds.
When supporting configuration is absent, class registration and initialization report unavailability and PTP registration yields no clock, allowing the driver to continue without those services.

PTP cross timestamp support is conditional. If platform parameters are unavailable the clock is still created without cross support. Otherwise device capability decides, and the cross operation is removed when unsupported.

Request messages are created with caller supplied sizes and identifier, with completion initialized, ownership preset for waiter plus completion path, and header identifier stored in device order. Failures release partial allocations and report lack of memory.
Virtqueue callbacks for request and alarm queues drain their respective queue through a shared loop, dispatching to response completion or alarm validation and forwarding.
RTC class operations expose time reading, alarm reading, alarm setting, and alarm interrupt control to the RTC core.
Alarm queue input is untrusted. Short headers, unknown types, and undersized alarm payloads are logged at limited rate and discarded, with the buffer still recycled so the queue keeps flowing.

Device exchanges can fail during allocation or transfer. Allocation failure reports lack of memory without transfer, transfer failure is logged for diagnosis, and message resources are released on all paths.
Alarm queue reposting can fail. Failure is reported as a warning while keeping the existing buffer handling intact, avoiding queue stall claims beyond the fragments.
Queue roles are ordered with request first and alarm second, followed by a total count. Device state sizes its queue array by that count.
Alarm queue buffers are sized to hold any alarm queue notification variant.
Timed device exchanges wait up to sixty seconds. Discovery exchanges for configuration and capabilities use no timeout.
